summary: Jesus gives the Twelve power and authority, sends them out with nothing for the road, and they go village by village.

context.title: The mission of the Twelve
paragraphs: Luke follows Mark’s account here, while Matthew gives a much fuller version of the instructions. [c1] The Twelve were chosen in Luke 6:13-16; now Jesus sends them out to preach and heal. [c2] Luke later tells of a second, larger mission of seventy (seventy-two in some manuscripts) in chapter 10, with several of the same instructions. [c3]

Jesus gives them both power and authority, the same pair the crowd used of his own word in Luke 4:36. [c4] The mission has two sides, proclaiming God’s kingdom and healing, and verse 6 shows them doing both. [c5] Mark adds that they were sent out two by two, which the Cambridge Bible takes as being for mutual support. [c6]

They travel without bag, bread or silver, and Luke, unlike Mark, forbids even a staff. [c7] The Cambridge Bible reads this as a call to go in the simplest manner and in perfect faith, relying on the open hospitality of the East. [c8] In each place they are to stay in one house rather than move from house to house. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Two Greek words: dynamis is the ability to act, exousia the right to act.
translationNotes.body: Dynamis is strength or ability, the power residing in someone by nature. [c10] Exousia comes from a verb meaning it is permitted, and its first sense is leave or permission. [c11] The Cambridge Bible puts the difference simply: the first is the capacity to act, the second the right to act. [c12] Jamieson, Fausset and Brown sum it up: Jesus both qualified and authorized them. [c13]

translationNotes.summary: The verb of sending gives the Twelve their title: apostles are those sent on a commission.
translationNotes.body: Apostellō means to send off, and Thayer uses it of persons sent with commissions. [c14] Luke has already named the Twelve apostoloi, the noun from this verb, when Jesus chose them in 6:13. [c15] The Cambridge Bible compares the Hebrew šĕlûḥîm, emissaries, and sees this mission as an important step in the training of the Twelve. [c16]

translationNotes.summary: The pēra was a leather bag for provisions; going without one meant depending on hosts for food.
translationNotes.body: Thayer defines the pēra as a leather sack in which travellers and shepherds carried their provisions. [c17] The Cambridge Bible pictures a bag slung over the shoulder holding a few dates or other necessaries. [c18] Without bag, bread or silver, the Twelve would eat what was given them wherever they came. [c19] At the Last Supper Jesus recalls this rule and then tells them to take a bag. [c20]

original.text: τὸν κονιορτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ποδῶν ὑμῶν ἀποτινάσσετε
original.translit: ton koniorton apo tōn podōn hymōn apotinassete
original.gloss: the dust from your feet shake off

translationNotes.summary: A gesture of separation: the messengers leave even a town’s dust behind as a witness.
translationNotes.body: Koniortos is properly dust raised or flying in the air, and then dust in general. [c21] Jewish purity teaching held that the very dust of a Gentile land carried defilement, which gave the gesture its weight. [c22] By it the messengers freed themselves of responsibility for a town’s refusal of their message. [c23] Paul and Barnabas make the same gesture at Pisidian Antioch in Acts 13:51. [c24]

claims.text: Luke’s account of the mission of the Twelve follows Mark, while Matthew 10:5-15 gives a much fuller account of the instructions.
The Twelve were chosen in Lk 6:13-16 and are sent out in Lk 9:1-6.
Some of the instructions to the Twelve are given again to the Seventy in Luke 10:1-16; the manuscripts vary between seventy and seventy-two.
In Lk 4:36 the crowd speaks of Jesus’ word acting with authority and power, the same pair of words as in Lk 9:1.
Lk 9:2 states the two objects of the mission, preaching the kingdom of God and healing, and Lk 9:6 reports both.
Mark 6:7 says Jesus sent them two by two, which the Cambridge Bible explains as for their mutual comfort.
Lk 9:3 forbids a staff, bag, bread and silver, whereas Mark 6:8 allows a staff only.
The Cambridge Bible reads the instructions as a call to go out in the simplest, humblest manner, with the Twelve’s small needs met by the open hospitality of the East.
Lk 9:4 directs them to stay in the same house the whole time they are in a place.
δύναμις means strength, ability, power, in general the inherent power residing in a person or thing.
ἐξουσία derives from ἔξεστι (it is permitted) and first means power of choice, leave or permission.
The Cambridge Bible distinguishes power (dunamis) as the capacity and authority (exousia) as the right to act.
Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say that by giving power and authority Jesus both qualified and authorized the Twelve.
ἀποστέλλω means to send off, and is used of persons sent with commissions.
In Lk 6:13 Jesus names the Twelve ἀπόστολοι.
The Cambridge Bible says the Twelve became, as their name implied, emissaries (sheloochim), and calls the mission an important step in their training.
A πήρα was a leather sack in which travellers and shepherds carried their provisions.
The Cambridge Bible describes the bag as carried over the shoulder to hold a few dates or other common necessaries.
Without bread or money the Twelve were to receive their food wherever they came.
In Lk 22:35-36 Jesus recalls sending them without a bag and then tells them to take one.
κονιορτός properly means raised or flying dust, and generally dust.
A Jewish maxim held that even the dust of a Gentile land brought defilement, which added to the significance of the gesture.
By shaking off the dust the messengers shook themselves free of all responsibility for the guilt of rejecting them and their message.
Paul and Barnabas shake the dust from their feet at Pisidian Antioch in Acts 13:51.
